_comment: C0 body translation · pyrit (2026-11-06). Key contract per cursor.en.json; sources/related counts must match the source file.

axes.model_access: Two sides both need models: the target under red-team, and the side driving the attacks. The repository front page names targets covering "OpenAI, Anthropic, Azure OpenAI, Microsoft Foundry, Azure Machine Learning, Google Gemini, Google Vertex AI, AWS Bedrock, Hugging Face, Ollama, Groq, OpenRouter, Cohere, and GitHub Copilot", with protocols written as "HTTP, WebSockets, browser automation with Playwright, or custom targets"; the docs 'latest' page compresses this into Any Target. On credentials the official wording is "PyRIT loads API credentials from environment variables or `.env` files", with OPENAI_CHAT_ENDPOINT / OPENAI_CHAT_KEY / OPENAI_CHAT_MODEL as the sample variables.
axes.runtime: Installed into your own Python environment: `pip install pyrit` (PyPI records requires-python >=3.10,<3.15, current version 1.1.0). The repository front page offers three entry points — a "command-line scanner", a "graphical interface" (CoPyRIT), and an "extensible Python framework"; the docs spell the CLI as `pyrit_scan` and `pyrit_shell`, and the GUI as interactive exploration with results reviewed in the browser. Execution happens on your own machine; whether any hosted execution surface exists: no official statement captured.
axes.local_files: It reads local configuration and `.env` credentials, and writes scan artefacts and state. The docs page states "Built-in Memory" has two backends, SQLite and Azure SQL — the first lands in a database file on your machine, the second in your own database. Default SQLite filename and path, plus cleanup and export methods: not verified word for word in this pass.
axes.background: Local semantics for long tasks are all present: adaptive multi-turn attacks and scenarios advance inside local processes, and results can be reviewed in the CoPyRIT interface (repository front page: "Explore AI systems interactively and review results in your browser"). A hosted queue that "keeps running after shutdown": not stated by the vendor — it is not a managed service.
axes.tools: Component surface on record in the docs: Automated Red Teaming (Crescendo and TAP named), Scenario Framework, Any Target, Built-in Memory, Flexible Scoring, plus the targets/converters/scorers/memory/orchestrators module split. The direct interface with another archive in this category: a dedicated docs page says the Garak scenario family "implements probes inspired by the Garak framework", run as `pyrit_scan run garak.prompt_inject --target openai_chat`. MCP support: not described in the official docs, recorded as unknown.
axes.context: Adaptive multi-turn attacks depend on revisitable conversation state, and that state lives in the memory backends above; the docs list "adaptive multi-turn attacks" alongside the scenario catalogue. The boundary of cross-session memory, and any compaction or truncation strategy: no itemised official text captured in this pass, recorded as unknown.
axes.permissions: Licence: MIT, copyright holder Microsoft (LICENSE read directly). Ownership needs one recorded fact: the original Azure/PyRIT repository page states "PyRIT has moved! Please see https://github.com/microsoft/PyRIT!", and this archive files the post-migration repository. Data flow: probe and attack prompts go to the target endpoint and the attack-model endpoint you configured, credentials are loaded from environment variables or `.env` (see the model_access axis), and run records land in your own SQLite/Azure SQL. Whether telemetry is on by default, and retention clauses: no official statement captured, moved to unknowns. It is an evaluation and forensics tool that does not block, so this site writes no "what share it stops" ratio and cites no scenario-report numbers.
axes.fit: Fits: orchestrating multi-turn adaptive attacks (Crescendo, TAP) into a repeatable assessment; needing to compose targets/converters/scorers yourself in Python; letting non-engineering reviewers go through results in a local GUI; teams already folding garak-style probes into one scan pipeline. Not a fit: wanting a single command that scans one endpoint and ends there (that is garak's default shape); needing hosted reports and compliance deliverables; expecting it to replace human red-team judgement.

runs:
**This site has not run it end to end**: no `pyrit_scan` execution and no CoPyRIT session, so no attack success rate, pass rate or ranking is produced, and the scenario count is not tallied. This archive only organises statements on record at the repository front page, LICENSE, the docs 'latest' page, two dedicated docs pages, releases and PyPI.

**Suggested measurements** (four):

- **What happens when only the target is configured and no attack model is** (the credential surface is on record; default behaviour is not)
- **Revisability differences between the SQLite and Azure SQL memory backends** (default file location and cleanup method not verified word for word)
- **Comparability between the Garak scenario family and native garak probe output** (the official framing is a ported implementation, not a garak call)
- **The capability gap between the CoPyRIT interface and `pyrit_scan`** (the GUI scenario catalogue is on record in the v1.1.0 notes; coverage not tallied)
unknowns:
- Whether any hosted execution surface (or hosted report service) exists: no official statement captured
- Default SQLite database filename and path, plus cleanup and export commands
- The boundary of cross-session memory and any context compaction/truncation strategy
- MCP transport support (not described in the official docs)
- Whether telemetry is on by default, and retention terms for scan records
- The itemised 0.x to v1.0.0 migration surface (only the release-notes headline was read)
- The capability gap between the CoPyRIT GUI scenario catalogue and the CLI scanners
- What actually happens when no attack/identity model is configured
- Mainland-network direct reachability and filing status (not measured, not searched)
related: Also a red-teaming framework: that archive is a terminal one-command scanner, this one is an orchestration framework with SDK/GUI/CLI entry points — and the official docs port garak's probes into this framework.
The other face of red teaming: this archive delivers an assessment pipeline you run yourself, Lakera delivers a hosted prevention API plus a red-team service.
A local endpoint: Ollama appears in the official target list, so a whole red-team run can stay inside your own network boundary.
